findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council carries £10.55m in on-call lending facilities callable at lender discretion
findings.detail: Two facilities are structured on-call with no fixed repayment dates: £10m from Middlesbrough Teeside Pension Fund at 3.85% (taken December 2025) and £550k from BG & Caerphilly at Bank Rate (outstanding since June 2012). Lenders can demand repayment on these facilities at any time, requiring the council to immediately refinance or find cash.
findings.matters: Prospective lenders assessing the council need to understand its refinancing risk and potential immediate cash requirements if on-call facilities are called
findings.figures: £10.55m in on-call facilities; largest facility £10m at 3.85%; total outstanding borrowing £80.55m
findings.quote: 19/12/2025 MIDDLESBROUGH TEESIDE PENSION FUND CALL / VARIABLE 10,000,000 3.85 ON CALL

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: The council borrowed £8.8m via PWLB in March 2026 at rates of 4.29–4.31%, comprising a maturity loan and an EIP facility.
findings.detail: On 09/03/2026 and 06/03/2026, the council drew £3.8m and £5m respectively on new PWLB facilities at 4.29% and 4.31%. Both loans are shown as fully drawn with repayment scheduled for 2027–2029. This recent borrowing indicates the council is actively investing or has identified a financing need.
findings.matters: Recent borrowing decisions signal the council's capital investment plans and funding requirements; lenders will want clarity on purpose and revenue plans to service new obligations.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: A PWLB maturity loan of £2.65m shows a repayment date of 16 June 2026, now three months overdue as of the report date.
findings.detail: The council borrowed £4m on 03/07/2001 at 5.13% with scheduled repayment on 16/06/2026. The loan still appears in the September 2026 schedule with an outstanding balance of £2.65m, suggesting the scheduled repayment date has passed. This could indicate an amortizing loan where interim payments have been made but final maturity has been missed, an undisclosed refinancing, or a data reporting lag.
findings.matters: A council showing scheduled debt obligations with past repayment dates and remaining outstanding balance is a credit concern; this requires explanation or remedial action.
findings.figures: Original value £4,000,000, current value £2,649,764.08, rate 5.13%, repayment date 16/06/2026

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: All borrowing is short-term from other councils and pension funds, at an average rate of 4.59%.
findings.detail: The schedule shows no PWLB or bond issuance: all £233m of borrowing is from other authorities and pension funds. Loans range from 1 to 184 days' duration. Interest rates across all borrowing average 4.59%, ranging from 4.0% to 6.1%. One facility from BG & Caerphilly (£550k) dated 2012 remains on-call at Bank of England base rate.
findings.matters: Short-term reliance creates refinancing risk. If market conditions tighten or lenders become less willing to roll facilities, the council faces pressure. A finance director would need to understand contingency plans and longer-term funding strategy.
findings.figures: Average Interest Rate 4.59%; total interest paid £3,142,857; rates range 4.0% to 6.1%
findings.quote: Average Interest Rate 4.59%

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: The council raised £174.5m of temporary loans in 2025/26, with £75.55m still outstanding at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: Borrowing brought forward from 2024/25 totalled £58.55m, of which £58m was repaid during the year leaving £550k outstanding. New loans of £174.5m were raised during 2025/26, of which £99.5m was repaid in the same year, leaving £75m outstanding. All borrowing is from other local authorities and pension funds. The pattern of £99.5m being raised and repaid within the same year indicates rolling short-term cash flow borrowing rather than permanent capital financing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's £75.55m outstanding balance reflects a temporary cash shortfall or a structural funding gap, and whether there is a credible plan to reduce it. The scale and rolling nature of this temporary borrowing is material to credit assessment.
findings.figures: £174.5m raised in 2025/26; £99.5m repaid in same year; £75.55m total outstanding at 31/03/2026; £550k brought forward outstanding

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council avoided long-term PWLB borrowing in Q1 due to high rates, using short-term loans instead.
findings.detail: No new long-term borrowing was undertaken in the first quarter as the council judged current PWLB rates to be unfavorable. The council repaid £2.6m of existing PWLB debt while raising £10m of new short-term loans from other local authorities via the marketplace. The council is retaining flexibility to lock in long-term borrowing if rates improve, demonstrating treasury discipline by declining to borrow at peak rates while managing capital needs through short-term borrowing.
findings.matters: Lenders assess whether a council makes disciplined capital financing decisions; avoiding borrowing at unfavorable rates reduces future refinancing costs and demonstrates prudent treasury management.
findings.figures: £2.6 million of PWLB debt repaid; £10 million of new short-term loans raised; £5 million of loans repaid.
findings.quote: No new long-term borrowing was undertaken during the period, as PWLB borrowing rates remained relatively high and did not represent value for money.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council drew £1.964m net from reserves in 2025/26, including £1.4m from Financial Resilience Reserve, to fund deficit
findings.detail: £1.4m drawn from Financial Resilience Reserve and £0.80m from Specific Reserves applied to cover £1.4m reported adverse variance. Net decrease in Specific Reserves of £1.964m across all reserve categories. Council explicitly warns this 'reduces the funding available to respond to future priorities and emerging risks.' Report states: 'The reliance on reserves to manage the in-year position reduces the funding available to respond to future service pressures, economic uncertainty and strategic priorities'.
findings.matters: Reserves are non-renewable; large repeated draws indicate underlying budget management challenge rather than temporary variance; reduces council's capacity to absorb future operational or strategic shocks; constrains flexibility for service improvement or innovation
findings.figures: £1.4m from Financial Resilience Reserve; £0.80m from Specific Reserves; £1.964m total net decrease in Specific Reserves; against approved budget of £201.5m
findings.quote: The financial position has required the application of reserves, including £0.80m of Specific Reserves and £1.4m from the Financial Resilience Reserve, reducing the level of funding available to respond to future priorities and emerging risks.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: School balances deteriorate to net deficit of £3.0m with 15 schools in deficit at year-end across all sectors
findings.detail: School balances declined by £1.7m during 2025/26, moving from net deficit of £1.275m to £2.976m. All sectors deteriorating: secondary deficits increased to £398k; all-through schools to £1.295m; primary schools shifted from £529k surplus to £566k deficit; special schools to £717k deficit. 15 schools held combined deficits of £4.0m. Pressures attributed to pay and utility costs. Council allocating additional £2.45m to schools in 2026/27 and £0.2m capital for energy efficiency to mitigate.
findings.matters: Threatens viability of school delegation framework; deterioration is systemic across all sectors rather than isolated to specific schools; growing structural deficit requiring sustained council intervention; constrains schools' ability to maintain or invest in services
findings.figures: £3.0m net deficit across all schools; £1.7m year-on-year deterioration; 15 schools in deficit; £4.0m combined school deficits
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the overall level of school balances has decreased by £1.7m, resulting in a net deficit position across all schools of £3m. A total of 15 schools were in deficit at year-end, with combined deficits amounting to £4m.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Children's Services reporting £3.14m adverse variance driven by placement cost escalation despite stable placement volume
findings.detail: The overspend is structural, driven by increasing complexity and intensity of children's needs rather than volume. Residential placements reported £1.5m adverse variance; the council's own children's home cannot accommodate externally-placed children due to complexity of their needs, preventing reduction of external placement spending. Placement income £0.19m short of forecast. Additional pressures from new fostering, supported living, and mother-and-baby placements, plus increased legal costs. Broader market pressures as private fostering providers leave the 4C's framework and move to independent pricing.
findings.matters: Statutory service with growing structural cost drivers independent of volume; complexity suggests demand controls alone will not resolve the issue; cost escalation trajectory unclear given structural nature of pressures
findings.figures: £3.14m adverse variance; £1.5m residential placements overspend; £0.19m income shortfall; £0.62m in other Children's Services overspend
findings.quote: Children, Young People & Families is reporting an adverse variance of £3.14m. This position reflects sustained demand-led pressures within Children's Services, particularly the continued increase in placement costs and the complex needs of children requiring care and support.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council achieved £378,381 favorable variance on net treasury costs, reversing Quarter 3 adverse forecast
findings.detail: Net treasury costs were £5,094,047 against budget of £5,472,428. The favorable swing was driven by strategic Q4 refinancing, higher investment returns, and effective cost management. The Council recovered from an adverse forecast position in Q3, demonstrating active treasury management during volatile interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Demonstrates overall treasury management competence and ability to navigate market volatility; improved financial position strengthens debt servicing capacity and validates strategic decisions
findings.figures: £378,381 favorable variance on net cost; total borrowing £206.99m (within £227.2m approved limit); no Operational Boundary breaches
findings.quote: Together with higher than anticipated investment income, this resulted in an overall favourable outturn and an improvement on the Quarter 3 forecast adverse position.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing rates averaged 4.59%, 84 basis points above 3.75% budget, incurring £1.38m excess cost
findings.detail: Market interest rates remained elevated throughout 2025/26 as the Bank of England cut rates more slowly than anticipated. The Council incurred £1,382,857 of excess costs on short-term borrowing. However, this adverse variance was fully offset by £1,438,889 in savings on long-term borrowing and £322k excess investment income, resulting in net favorable treasury outturn of £378,381.
findings.matters: Exposes Council's vulnerability to sustained market rate elevation, but demonstrates capacity to manage rate risk through strategic refinancing and investment returns
findings.figures: 4.59% actual rate vs 3.75% benchmark; £1,382,857 adverse variance on short-term borrowing; £3,142,857 total short-term borrowing costs
findings.quote: During the financial year, the Authority paid an average interest rate of 4.59% on temporary or short term borrowings, compared to a benchmark rate of 3.75% based on budget assumptions. This resulted in total borrowing costs of £3,142,857.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council investment income outperformed budget by £322,339, generating £592,839 against forecast £270,500
findings.detail: The Council placed £375.55m in temporary investments at an average return of 3.97%, exceeding the 3.73% benchmark rate. This outperformance reflects effective management of the investment portfolio within approved Treasury Management Strategy constraints, prioritising security and liquidity while generating returns above benchmark.
findings.matters: Demonstrates effective cash management and ability to generate above-benchmark returns; the income outperformance helped offset elevated short-term borrowing costs
findings.figures: £592,839 actual vs £270,500 budget (119% of forecast); 3.97% average return vs 3.73% benchmark; £375.55m total invested
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, investment income totals £592,839, exceeding the full‑year budget of £270,500.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council refinanced £8.8m from short-term to long-term borrowing in Q4 2025/26 before PWLB rates increased again
findings.detail: In Q4, the Council undertook £8.8m of new PWLB borrowing at 4.30% average rate to replace maturing short-term debt, securing funding as market rates briefly eased. The paper describes this as prudent timing: PWLB rates subsequently increased towards end of March, validating the decision and reducing the Council's refinancing risk exposure.
findings.matters: Shows active refinancing management and ability to access capital markets; demonstrates awareness of interest rate risk and successful execution of timing strategy
findings.figures: £8.8m long-term borrowing at 4.30% average rate; total long-term debt outstanding £131.44m
findings.quote: In Quarter 4, the Council undertook £8.8 million of new long-term borrowing from the PWLB to refinance maturing short-term debt and provide greater certainty over future borrowing costs. This decision was considered prudent, as it secured long-term funding at a point when market rates had shown signs of easing, before PWLB rates increased again towards the end of March 2026.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Education portfolio identifies £192k Funding Cost Pressures—a new pressure line not in the original budget
findings.detail: A line item for Funding Cost Pressures within the education portfolio shows £192.1k forecast, with £0 budgeted. This emerging pressure suggests cost inflation within education not anticipated at budget setting.
findings.matters: A newly-identified pressure line indicates emerging cost inflation or other service pressures within education that were not fully anticipated.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council Tax Collection generating £360k favourable variance, providing partial offset to service pressures
findings.detail: Forecast income £1.45m against budget £1.09m—33% better collection than anticipated. This favourable variance provides some cashflow benefit.
findings.matters: Stronger-than-expected collection helps offset the material demand-driven overspends elsewhere in the budget.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: ICT Service forecast to overspend by £214k—a 570% variance with no explanation in the document
findings.detail: Budgeted at £37.6k, forecast to cost £251.7k. This extreme percentage variance suggests either severe budget underestimation or unplanned expenditure, but the document provides no explanation of the cause.
findings.matters: A 570% variance on a support service, even at modest absolute value, signals either structural underestimation of ongoing IT costs or material one-off pressures requiring explanation.
findings.figures: Budget £37,630; forecast £251,746; variance £214,116

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Children, Young People & Families portfolio forecast for £2.62m adverse variance, with demand pressures spreading across multiple services
findings.detail: Portfolio budget £94.15m but forecast £97.29m. Beyond Children Looked After (£2.76m over), Other Children's and Family Services shows £0.62m overspend and Supporting Special Education Needs £0.04m over. This £3.14m total adverse variance is only partially offset by favourable variances in other council services.
findings.matters: This portfolio represents one of the largest budget areas in the council. Systematic demand pressures across multiple service lines indicate the budget underestimated service need.
findings.figures: Portfolio budget £94,151,770; forecast £97,291,664; variance £3,139,894

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Children Looked After forecast to overspend by £2.76m, the largest single budget variance across the council
findings.detail: The service, budgeted at £7.42m, is forecast to cost £10.18m by March 2026—a 37% overspend. The position has worsened since December by approximately £350k, indicating demand continues to exceed budget assumptions.
findings.matters: Children Looked After is demand-driven and statutory; the council cannot refuse placements. An overspend of this scale indicates demand that could not be managed within budget and creates material financial risk.
findings.figures: Budget £7,423,930; forecast £10,179,915; variance £2,755,985

findings.detail: Additional Welsh Government funding was awarded to Coal Tip Safety scheme in the final quarter, bringing new money into remediation of environmental liabilities.
findings.matters: Securing external funding for environmental remediation reduces burden on council reserves and shows Welsh Government confidence in council's delivery.

findings.matters: Project slippage corrections show whether committed capital schemes are progressing or stalling; this one is now cleared.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council approved £6.3 million in Transforming Towns regeneration funding in Q4 2025/26.
findings.detail: Four major urban regeneration schemes received new Welsh Government and Shared Prosperity Fund (SPF) approval in the final quarter: Old Abertillery Library Refurbishment (£1.85m), Gwent Shopping Centre (£1.52m), Metropole External Improvements (£608k), and Ebbw Vale Multi Storey (£2.31m). All recorded as new funding in Q4.
findings.matters: A £6.3m surge in regeneration funding approvals in a single quarter indicates significant external investment secured and the council's capacity to deliver major capital schemes.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Net favourable capital variance of £82,861 achieved despite slippage and overspends.
findings.detail: After accounting for £6.5m slippage and £80,368 in scheme overspends, the capital programme ended net favourable. This indicates the council successfully managed its overall capital envelope by reallocating resources between schemes.
findings.matters: The favourable net position demonstrates financial control and the council's ability to adjust spending in real time to stay within its capital envelope, supporting confidence in financial management.
findings.figures: £82,861 net favourable variance
findings.quote: Proposed slippage of £6.5m leaves a net favourable variance of £82,861.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Four capital schemes exceeded budget with combined overspends of £80,368.
findings.detail: Emergency Funding - Flood Aleviation overspent by £28,212, TT - The Metropole External Improvements by £25,767, WPT - General Offices by £18,955, and unbudgeted Civic Centre Decommissioning added £7,434. These were funded through reallocation of slippage from underspent schemes and external grants.
findings.matters: Recurring overspends across multiple schemes indicate project cost control or forecasting challenges that a lender would want to understand when assessing the council's ability to deliver on budget.
findings.figures: £80,368 total overspends: Flood Aleviation £28,212, Metropole £25,767, General Offices £18,955, Civic Centre £7,434

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: £6.5m of capital budget slipped to 2026/27, representing 13.6% of planned in-year spending.
findings.detail: The council spent £41.1m of its £47.7m in-year capital budget (86.2% delivery rate). £6.5m of funding was proposed to move into the next financial year because projects or payments were delayed. This scale of slippage signals material delays in planned capital delivery.
findings.matters: Slippage of this magnitude affects cash flow timing, project delivery pace, and the council's ability to deploy capital as planned—important for understanding whether commitments underpinning borrowing decisions are being met.
findings.figures: £6.5m slippage against £47.7m in-year budget
findings.quote: At outturn, capital expenditure was £41.1m against the £47.7m in-year budget. Proposed slippage of £6.5m leaves a net favourable variance of £82,861.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: After accounting for slippage, capital programme achieved net favourable variance of £82,861.
findings.detail: Despite underspending of £6.6m, slippage of £6.5m, and overspends of £80k in individual schemes, the overall capital programme remained within total approved resources. The net break-even position indicates effective overall budget management.
findings.matters: Confirms council did not overspend its approved capital budget overall, demonstrating financial discipline despite individual scheme variances.
findings.figures: £82,861 net favourable variance (£0.083m)
findings.quote: After taking account of the proposed slippage, the Capital Programme reports a net favourable variance of £82,861 (£0.083m), indicating that the programme has remained within available resources.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital programme funding increased by £10.2m since Quarter 3, predominantly from external grants.
findings.detail: Funding increase comprised £9.8m in additional external grant funding and £0.4m from council resources. This mid-year improvement in financing position came from securing grants rather than internal reallocation.
findings.matters: Shows council successfully attracted additional external funding during the year, improving overall capital financing position.
findings.figures: £10.2m total increase; £9.8m external grants, £0.4m council resources
findings.quote: Funding increased by approximately £10.2m since Quarter 3, of which £9.8m related to additional external grant funding and £0.4m related to contributions from Council resources.

findings.headline: Four capital schemes overspent by £80,368 total, but overspends were accommodated within available resources.
findings.detail: Overspends occurred in Flood Alleviation (£28,212), Transforming Towns Metropole (£25,767), Workplace Transformation (£18,955), and Civic Centre Decommissioning (£7,434). These were funded through reallocation from programme underspends or revenue contributions, with no additional funding approvals required.
findings.matters: Demonstrates specific capital schemes exceeded budget, but shows council had sufficient financial flexibility to manage overruns without requesting additional resources.
findings.figures: £80,368 total overspends; largest: £28,212 (Flood Alleviation), £25,767 (Metropole), £18,955 (Workplace)
findings.quote: Four schemes reported overspends at year end totalling £80,368. Following these funding adjustments, all identified overspends were accommodated within available resources and no additional funding approvals were required.

findings.committee: Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee

findings.detail: Total capital expenditure was £41.120m against an in-year budget of £47.722m. Proposed slippage of £6.519m reflects ongoing schemes where expenditure has been reprofiled into 2026/27, indicating a significant volume of work not yet complete.
findings.matters: Indicates council's capital delivery rate and signals that substantial funded work will require completion in the next financial year.
findings.figures: £41.120m spent vs £47.722m budgeted (86.2% delivery); £6.519m slippage
findings.quote: Total capital expenditure was £41.120m against an in-year budget of £47.722m, representing a delivery rate of 86.2%. Proposed slippage of £6.519m reflects schemes that remain in progress and where funding is required to be carried forward in 2026/2027.

findings.matters: This provision reveals the council's exposure to interest rate movements and its expectation that rates will not fall; it affects the council's debt sustainability assessment.

findings.matters: School balances are meant for educational delivery; using them to cover council overspends signals financial stress and raises questions about whether schools can maintain planned services.

findings.matters: Reserves are a lender's second line of defence; their depletion signals reduced financial resilience and a narrower margin for managing future pressures.

findings.matters: A lender funding this council would care about budget overspends and whether they are structural or one-off, and whether reserve buffers are adequate.

findings.headline: Social care system replacement carries a High risk of service disruption and statutory non-compliance if implementation fails
findings.detail: CRR32 identifies the Mosaic system (replacing legacy WCCIS) as a High corporate risk. The Council explicitly notes that implementation failure could cause service disruption, data integrity loss, failure to meet statutory reporting obligations and direct risk to vulnerable people.
findings.matters: Social care is typically a major budget commitment and immovable statutory responsibility; system implementation failure creates both service quality and regulatory compliance risks
findings.figures: no financial impact figures provided in the paper
findings.quote: There is a risk that if the Mosaic social care system is not successfully implemented as a replacement for WCCIS this will result in disruption to service delivery, compromised data integrity, and non-compliance with statutory reporting and operational requirements putting vulnerable people at risk.

findings.headline: Staff absence remains a High corporate risk despite ongoing management, with explicit impact on service delivery and financial performance
findings.detail: CRR14 remains High-rated and on the Corporate Risk Register. The Council's own risk description makes clear that failure to improve attendance directly damages both operational capacity and the financial position. The fact that this remains High through year-end despite being tracked as a corporate risk suggests it is persistent.
findings.matters: High sickness absence increases staffing costs, reduces the council's service delivery capacity and prevents reallocation of resources to savings plans; it signals potential workforce morale or management issues
findings.figures: sickness absence performance data for 2025/26 detailed in Appendix B (not reproduced in this extract)
findings.quote: Failure to improve staff attendance rates within the Council will lead to an unacceptable impact on the ability of the Council to deliver services effectively and financially.

findings.headline: Financial resilience risk has been expanded to explicitly incorporate increasing demand, inflation and complexity of need across statutory services
findings.detail: CRR21 has been revised and remains High-rated. The Council amended the wording to explicitly recognise that increasing demand, inflationary pressures and rising complexity of need across statutory services are strategic threats to long-term financial stability. This change folded in the financial drivers previously tracked as a separate Critical risk (CRR20, Children's Services Sustainability, which remains Critical in score but de-escalated from the corporate register).
findings.matters: Demand-led and inflationary pressures across multiple statutory services indicate structural financial challenges beyond one-time savings; they limit financial headroom and may require service reductions or new funding sources
findings.figures: no quantified demand or inflation figures provided in the paper
findings.quote: The financial resilience and sustainability of the Council could be at risk if financial planning, resource allocation and management decisions are unable to respond effectively to increasing demand, inflationary pressures and the rising complexity of need within statutory services, thereby compromising the Council's long-term financial stability.

findings.headline: School deficits are rated as a Critical corporate risk threatening the Council's ability to sustain education services
findings.detail: CRR34 is the only Critical risk on the register at year-end, specifically identifying projected school deficits as the primary driver of a risk that the Council will be unable to sustain education services and deliver positive outcomes for children. This is the highest risk designation the Council applies.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that a council can sustain core statutory services; education deficits signal structural financial strain that may force difficult service trade-offs or require new borrowing sources
findings.figures: no quantified deficit figures provided in the paper
findings.quote: There is a risk that the Council will be unable to sustain education services and deliver positive outcomes for children and young people, caused by financial constraints and projected school deficits.

findings.headline: £4.48m match funding for schools programme based on high-level estimates with cost uncertainty
findings.detail: The Sustainable Communities for Learning programme includes £4.48m of council match funding for Welsh Government grants, but the paper notes final costs, delivery timescales and affordability are subject to approval of detailed business cases. This creates cost overrun risk.
findings.matters: Final costs for a major programme are uncertain and could require additional funding if Welsh Government contributions or final costs change.
findings.figures: £4.48m match funding proposed
findings.quote: This provision is based on high-level estimates, with the final funding requirement, delivery timescales and affordability implications subject to the approval of individual detailed business cases.

findings.headline: Council using £0.86m from earmarked reserves to fund capital schemes
findings.detail: Specific earmarked reserves totalling £0.86m have been allocated to support specific capital schemes within the programme. This reduces the council's available reserve buffers.
findings.matters: Drawing reserves for capital investment reduces financial resilience and the council's ability to respond to unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: £0.86m from specific reserves
findings.quote: Specific Reserve Funding £0.86m – set aside to support specific schemes

findings.headline: Programme depends on generating £0.3m annual capital receipts which may not materialise
findings.detail: The funding plan assumes £0.3m of capital receipts will be generated per annum, with £7.3m total receipts funding prior years' slippage. If asset sales underperform this assumption, the funding gap widens further.
findings.matters: If capital receipts assumptions fail, the already-identified £0.8m shortfall becomes worse and forces deeper programme cuts.
findings.figures: £0.3m per annum assumed; £7.3m total capital receipts
findings.quote: Useable Capital receipts £7.3m – to fund prior years slippage and it has been assumed that £0.3m capital receipts will be generated per annum to support capital investment

findings.headline: Council approving £0.4m prudential borrowing for schools digital infrastructure
findings.detail: The programme includes £0.4m of new prudential borrowing to support digital infrastructure investment in schools. This adds to the council's debt burden and creates ongoing revenue servicing costs.
findings.matters: New borrowing increases the council's debt servicing costs from revenue and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £0.4m prudential borrowing
findings.quote: Prudential Borrowing of £0.4m to support digital infrastructure in schools.

findings.headline: Community Equipment & Adaptations costs rising £140,000 annually due to demand pressures
findings.detail: Investment in this service area has increased by £140,000 per annum to reflect identified demand pressures and service requirements, signalling sustained cost growth in this budget line.
findings.matters: Growing demand in a frontline service suggests this cost pressure will likely persist, creating ongoing budget pressure.
findings.figures: £140,000 per annum increase
findings.quote: Investment in Community Equipment & Adaptations has increased by £140,000 per annum to reflect demand pressures and service requirements.

findings.headline: £9.1m capital slippage from 2025/2026 indicates delivery challenges
findings.detail: The council carried forward £9.1m of undelivered capital investment from the prior year, approved by the Leadership Team after detailed programme delivery review. This substantial slippage suggests capacity or planning constraints that may carry forward into the new programme.
findings.matters: Significant carry-forward indicates delivery challenges in the previous year; similar issues could affect the new programme's ability to deploy £38m as planned.
findings.figures: £9.1m carry-forward from 2025/2026
findings.quote: Following a detailed review of programme delivery, the Leadership Team approved the carry forward (slippage) of £9.1m from 2025/2026 to support the continuation of approved capital schemes.

findings.headline: Capital programme identifies £0.8m funding shortfall across five years
findings.detail: The £38m proposed capital programme has an overall funding shortfall of £0.8m, with £2m shortfall within the first three years and £0.5m in 2026/2027. The council is exploring external funding, reserve use, and reprioritisation as solutions, but explicitly notes this represents a financial and deliverability risk requiring active ongoing management.
findings.matters: Inability to fully fund the agreed programme creates deliverability risk and may force difficult reprioritisation of investments or draw additional reserves.
findings.figures: £0.8m shortfall over 5 years; £2m shortfall first 3 years; £0.5m in 2026/2027
findings.quote: The proposed Strategic Capital Programme identifies an overall funding shortfall of £0.8m across the life of the programme, including a shortfall of £2m within the first three years and £0.5m in 2026/2027.

findings.paper_title: SCO2603D4 Blueprint for Growth - External Funding Report
findings.headline: Uncertainty exists about whether local delivery will be constrained by alignment with national and regional programmes.
findings.detail: The council notes "There is concern that local delivery may be required to align with national and regional programmes, potentially limiting the ability to respond to local needs, priorities, and aspirations." This uncertainty was formally raised with Welsh Government as part of the consultation response.
findings.matters: Constraints on local control could mean Blaenau Gwent cannot direct funding to its own highest priorities, reducing the return on investment and limiting responsiveness to council-identified need.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: There is concern that local delivery may be required to align with national and regional programmes, potentially limiting the ability to respond to local needs, priorities, and aspirations.

findings.paper_title: SCO2603D4 Blueprint for Growth - External Funding Report
findings.headline: Substantial officer capacity requirement to deliver complex funding programmes.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges "These are considerable and complex funding packages with associated substantial delivery programmes attached to them. It is important that there is sufficient officer capacity available to ensure the delivery of the various projects." Delivery teams will be funded through a combination of council core funding and grant awards.
findings.matters: Capacity constraints could lead to poor project delivery, compliance failures, or unused funding. The fact the council must fund management teams from its own resources or the grants suggests budget pressure on delivery capacity.
findings.figures: None specified, but programme and project management teams will be funded from combination of core council funding and grant awards
findings.quote: These are considerable and complex funding packages with associated substantial delivery programmes attached to them. It is important that there is sufficient officer capacity available to ensure the delivery of the various projects.

findings.paper_title: SCO2603D4 Blueprint for Growth - External Funding Report
findings.headline: Revenue funding of only £2.8m significantly limits the scope to deliver employment and skills programmes.
findings.detail: The 70/30 capital-to-revenue split means only £2,802,243 is available for revenue programmes. The council explicitly states this "significantly limits the scope to deliver programmes that support people back into work and underpin the capital programme."
findings.matters: The revenue constraint may limit the council's ability to achieve the stated economic objectives of supporting job creation and skills development, undermining the return on capital investment.
findings.figures: £2,802,243 revenue funding out of £9,358,788 total (30%)
findings.quote: The relatively low level of revenue funding significantly limits the scope to deliver programmes that support people back into work and underpin the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: SCO2603D4 Blueprint for Growth - External Funding Report
findings.headline: Capital funding (70% of allocation) presents high delivery risk within a one-year spend timeframe.
findings.detail: £6.56m of the £9.36m allocation is capital that must be spent by March 2027. The council explicitly acknowledges "the high proportion of capital funding presents challenges in terms of spend within a one-year programme timeframe" and recognises that "Delivering new capital projects from inception will be particularly challenging given the time required to secure permissions, procure contractors, and complete construction."
findings.matters: Unspent grant funding may need to be returned to Welsh Government, wasting development opportunity and potentially harming the council's relationship with future funders. The council is mitigating by focusing on existing projects only.
findings.figures: £6,556,545 capital (70% of allocation); £2,802,243 revenue (30%)
findings.quote: The high proportion of capital funding presents challenges in terms of spend within a one‑year programme timeframe. This is likely to necessitate a focus on existing projects that are already in delivery. Delivering new capital projects from inception will be particularly challenging given the time required to secure permissions, procure contractors, and complete construction.

findings.paper_title: SCO2603D4 Blueprint for Growth - External Funding Report
findings.headline: The £9.36m Local Growth Fund allocation remains indicative with no formal funding agreement yet issued.
findings.detail: Blaenau Gwent is planning around an indicative allocation of £9,358,788 for 2026/27, but the council acknowledges allocations to individual authorities are unconfirmed and no formal regional funding agreement has been issued. This creates material uncertainty around whether the full amount will actually be received.
findings.matters: Capital commitments and the economic growth strategy depend on this funding being confirmed. If allocations are reduced, the council's delivery plans would need to be scaled back significantly.
findings.figures: £9,358,788 indicative allocation for 2026/27 (comprising £2,802,243 revenue and £6,556,545 capital) within £79,787,415 regional allocation
findings.quote: Allocations to individual local authorities remain indicative, and it is therefore unclear what funding each council will ultimately receive. No formal regional funding agreement has yet been issued

findings.paper_title: SCO2603D7 Appendix A - Treasury Strategy Statement 2026-27.docx
findings.headline: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream trending upward from 3.67% (2024/25 actual) to 3.89% (2026/27 estimate)
findings.detail: The affordability indicator tracking debt servicing costs as a percentage of net revenue is rising: 3.67% actual in 2024/25, 3.81% estimate in 2025/26, and 3.89% in 2026/27. After 2026/27 it holds or slightly declines (3.81% in 2027/28, 3.69% in 2028/29), but the near-term trend is upward despite the council being under-borrowed.
findings.matters: Even with internal borrowing reducing external debt, the cost of servicing debt is growing as a proportion of revenue. This constrains financial flexibility and indicates rising debt service pressure, likely from combination of higher rates and existing debt maturity profiles.
findings.quote: The estimates of financing costs for 2026/2027 include current commitments and the proposals in the budget report presented to Council in February/March

findings.paper_title: SCO2603D7 Appendix A - Treasury Strategy Statement 2026-27.docx
findings.headline: Council is under-borrowed and using internal cash reserves to fund capital spending, with external borrowing deferred despite rising rates
findings.detail: The council's actual debt (£204.674m in 2025/26) is substantially below its Capital Financing Requirement (£219.715m in 2025/26), creating an under-borrowed position of £13.094m. The council is deliberately using internal cash balances to fund capital expenditure instead of external borrowing, described as cost-effective while rates are elevated. The liability benchmark shows a projected borrowing gap that will require future external funding as the under-borrowed position persists.
findings.matters: Running down internal resources to avoid borrowing at high rates is a temporary strategy. At some point this will reverse, and the council will need to borrow at whatever rates prevail. The document signals this is planned but the timing and cost are uncertain.
findings.figures: External debt 2025/26: £204.674m; CFR 2025/26: £219.715m; under/over borrowing: £13.094m. Liability benchmark 2025/26: £207.432m; existing loan debt: £204.674m; projected under-borrowed position 2026/27: £81.090m
findings.quote: This reflects the Council's continued use of internal cash balances to fund capital expenditure instead of taking external loans, thereby reducing interest costs while market borrowing rates remain elevated

findings.paper_title: SCO2603D7 Appendix A - Treasury Strategy Statement 2026-27.docx
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast to fall 40% from £45.985m (2025/26) to £27.761m (2026/27), with no explanation provided
findings.detail: The capital programme drops sharply from £45.985m in 2025/26 to £27.761m in 2026/27, a reduction of £18.2m or 39.6%, with further declines to £26.460m in 2027/28 and £18.647m in 2028/29. The document presents these figures without explaining the driver of such a significant contraction.
findings.matters: A sudden 40% cut in capital spending signals either completed major schemes, budget constraint, delivery delays, or changed strategic priorities. A lender needs to understand whether this reflects completion of planned work or reduced capacity to deliver the council's asset strategy.
findings.figures: 2025/26 capital expenditure estimate £45,985k; 2026/27 estimate £27,761k; 2027/28 estimate £26,460k; 2028/29 estimate £18,647k
findings.quote: Estimated figures for 2026/26, 2027//28 & 2028/29 are based on the Authority's approved capital programme plus external funding approvals received at this stage and estimated spending

findings.paper_title: CO2603D8 Treasury Management Mid Year Review - September 2025
findings.headline: £11.2m of long-term debt maturing in 2026/27 requires refinancing ahead of expected rate improvement
findings.detail: The council repaid £12m in market loans during the first half and faces £11.2m of long-term debt maturity in 2026/27. Treasury staff are actively exploring refinancing options ahead of this maturity. The council expects improved market conditions as Bank of England rates soften, but refinancing costs will depend on whether actual conditions match this forecast.
findings.matters: A specific refinancing point in 2026/27; if interest rates remain elevated or rise further, the council will face higher costs than budgeted for this roll-over
findings.figures: £11.2m maturing 2026/27, £12m repaid in H1, total long-term debt £130.3m, total external debt £198.9m
findings.quote: However, the Council repaid £12m in Market loans and has £11.2m of long‑term debt maturing in 2026/27. The Treasury Management team are actively exploring refinancing options ahead of this maturity.

findings.paper_title: CO2603D8 Treasury Management Mid Year Review - September 2025
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing costs forecast £2.090m above budget due to sustained elevated interest rates
findings.detail: Short-term borrowing costs are projected at £3.850m, exceeding the £1.760m budget by £2.090m, driven by an average rate of 4.35%. The council has deliberately continued using short-term borrowing while long-term PWLB rates remain elevated, to avoid locking into unfavorable fixed rates. This overspend is partially offset by a £1.584m underspend on long-term borrowing and strong investment income.
findings.matters: Material unbudgeted borrowing costs reduce resources available for services; the decision to use expensive short-term funding reflects expectations that rates will improve, but carries refinancing risk if they do not
findings.figures: £2.090m above budget (forecast £3.850m vs budget £1.760m), average rate 4.35%, Bank of England rates fell from 4.50% to 4.00% during the period
findings.quote: Short‑term borrowing costs are forecast to be £2.090m above budget due to elevated temporary borrowing rates, which have remained higher for longer as a result of the slower‑than‑expected reduction in Bank of England base rates.

findings.headline: Council Tax survey showed only 36% support for proposed increase; limited headroom for further tax rises.
findings.detail: The council's public engagement survey (127 respondents) found that 64% did not support the initial assumption of 4.95% Council Tax increase. The council has settled on 3.75%. This low support indicates limited political room to raise tax further if savings plans (school reorganisation, Federation efficiencies) fail to deliver.
findings.matters: If savings plans do not materialise and the council cannot raise tax (due to public resistance), the gap will widen with no obvious funding source. A 1% reduction in Council Tax increases the gap by £318k, per the risk section.
findings.figures: 127 survey respondents; 64% opposed 4.95% increase; approved increase: 3.75%; 1% reduction = £318k additional gap
findings.quote: 64% of respondents did not support the initial assumption of a 4.95% increase in Council Tax.

findings.headline: Medium-term gap of £8.7m remains unresolved over 2027-2031; MTFS assumes only £3m per annum in cost pressures but provides no detail on funding sources.
findings.detail: After bridging the 2026/2027 gap of £3.9m, the council faces a cumulative 5-year gap of £12.6m, of which £8.7m remains unaddressed beyond 2026/2027. The MTFS assumes £3m per annum in cost pressures for 2027/2028 onwards, but the document provides no outline of planned savings to offset this recurring deficit.
findings.matters: A balanced budget for one year built on one-off mitigations (reserves, unproven school reorganisation) signals forward-year sustainability risk. The council has not published a believable plan to deliver £3m annual savings in years 2-5.
findings.figures: Cumulative 5-year gap: £12.6m; 2026/2027 gap: £3.9m; remaining 4-year gap: £8.7m; assumed ongoing cost pressures: £3m per annum 2027/2028 onwards
findings.quote: Looking ahead, financial challenges will continue beyond 2026/2027. Current modelling indicates the need to deliver approximately £8.7m of savings over the following four years.

findings.headline: Pay award risk: a 1% swing above the 3% assumption costs £1.2m and eats a third of the annual budget gap.
findings.detail: The budget assumes 3% pay awards for all staff. The document explicitly flags that 'if pay awards are higher than the current assumption of 3%, this will result in an in-year cost pressure for 2026/2027 and impact on the funding gap in future years.' A 1% variation costs £1.2m across all services including schools.
findings.matters: The 2026/2027 budget gap is only £3.9m. A 1% pay award variance of £1.2m is material—one-third of the gap. If public sector pay grows beyond 3%, the council has limited headroom to absorb it without cutting services or raising tax further.
findings.figures: 3% pay assumption; 1% variance = £1.2m impact; total 2026/2027 gap = £3.925m
findings.quote: The Pay awards are higher than the current assumption of 3% applied to the draft estimates. A higher pay ward will result in an in-year cost pressure for 2026/2027 and impact on the funding gap in future years. The financial impact of a 1% change in the assumption is approximately £1.2m, across all services including schools.

findings.headline: Transitional reserve funding of £2m committed in 2026/2027 to prop up Children's Services cost pressures while 'steps are taken to mitigate'.
findings.detail: The council is using earmarked reserves to fund a £2m transitional payment in 2026/2027 (and further £0.75m in 2027/2028) to cover increased costs for children looked after whilst the council develops mitigation plans. The language 'whilst steps are taken to mitigate' suggests this is interim funding pending real savings delivery, which may not materialise.
findings.matters: Deploying reserves to absorb demand-led service pressures signals structural deficit in that service area, not a one-off adjustment. Children's services is a statutory, demand-led budget—if costs are outpacing income, the council is managing a structural problem via reserve drawdown, which is unsustainable.
findings.figures: £2m transitional funding 2026/2027; £0.75m further tranche 2027/2028; earmarked reserves forecast to decline from £29.042m to £26.315m by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: In setting the 2026/20027 budget, transitional funding of up to £2m has been committed (with a further £0.75m for 2027/2028) to support: Children's Services with the increased costs for children looked after, whilst steps are taken to mitigate the cost pressure.

findings.headline: School reorganisation programme to stabilise finances is still under development, not yet agreed; if not delivered, deficits will grow and council must cut other services.
findings.detail: To address school deficits, the council proposes 'a programme of review under development' covering estate rationalisation, school federations, and shared leadership. This is explicitly conditional: 'If business case proposals for school reorganisation and rationalisation are not developed and agreed to support financial stability, deficit balances will continue to grow... Alternatively, funding allocations to schools would need to increase beyond annual pay pressures to maintain service levels. If the latter approach is taken this would necessitate reductions or the cessation of other Council Services.'
findings.matters: The council's financial plan depends on a savings scheme that has no approved business case and no implementation timeline. If it fails, the council must either allow schools to deteriorate or raid other services—both material risks to creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £3.8m deficit to resolve; unquantified savings target from school reorganisation
findings.quote: To support schools in achieving financial stability and mitigate deficit balances, a programme of review is under development to identify opportunities including reducing the school estate where surplus capacity exists, federate schools to share leadership, resources and administrative functions and reduce the number of buildings to lower maintenance and operational costs.

findings.headline: School deficits growing despite £6.35m funding uplift, forecast to reach £3.8m by March 2026.
findings.detail: The council is providing schools with a 10% uplift (£6.35m) to cover pay pressures and rebalance budgets. Despite this, school deficits are forecast to increase by around £2.5m to £3.8m by March 2026. Schools face declining pupil numbers creating surplus places, growing demand for additional learning needs, and rising operational costs that the council is asking schools to absorb.
findings.matters: Persistent deficits in a core council service suggest structural misalignment between provision and demand, and the S151 officer explicitly flags this as 'a significant concern'—implying the problem cannot be solved by incremental adjustments.
findings.figures: Deficit forecast to reach £3.8m by March 2026; £6.35m (10%) uplift to Individual Schools Budget for 2026/2027; schools expected to absorb £0.3m of non-pay cost pressures
findings.quote: School deficits are forecast to increase by around £2.5m to £3.8m by March 2026 despite the additional funding approved by Council. Schools are finding it increasingly challenging in balancing their budgets due to: Declining pupil numbers, resulting in surplus places in some settings and reducing pupil led funding; Growing demand for additional learning needs; Rising operational costs

findings.headline: Several financial institutions downgraded in recent years, forcing council to withdraw investment from higher-yield counterparties
findings.detail: Multiple counterparties have been downgraded by credit rating agencies and no longer meet the council's investment criteria. As a result, the council has ceased investing in institutions offering higher rates and is prioritizing capital preservation instead. This constrains investment options and is why the council's return of 4.69% fell 18bps short of the 4.87% benchmark—a direct impact of reduced counterparty availability.
findings.matters: Downgrade pressure on the council's investment counterparties signals broader credit stress and reduces the pool of acceptable borrowers for temporary lending, which directly affects the council's ability to deploy cash at competitive rates
findings.figures: Investment return 4.69% vs benchmark 4.87% (18bps shortfall); £3m invested as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: the Authority has ceased investing in counterparties offering higher rates due to recent reductions in their credit ratings, prioritising capital preservation and risk management

findings.headline: Council replaced PWLB long-term loans with temporary borrowing at higher rates, betting on interest rate falls in 2025-26
findings.detail: The council repaid £14.05m in long-term PWLB loans and replaced them with short-term borrowing from other local authorities at 5.14% average, well above the 3.50% budget assumption. The strategy assumes rates will fall in 2025-26, making temporary borrowing preferable to locking in long-term rates above the council's historical average of 3.84%. If rates fall as forecast, this saves money; if they don't, the council faces higher refinancing costs and must revisit the strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this bet on interest rate movements is prudent or a material risk, and whether the council has fallback plans if rates remain elevated
findings.figures: £148m short-term loans raised at 5.14% average; £14.05m PWLB repaid; £12m market loans maturing H1 2025-26; long-term rate 3.84%, budget assumption 3.50%
findings.quote: The increase in short-term borrowing costs is primarily attributable to the strategic repayment of long-term Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) loans. These were replaced with temporary loans, as long-term borrowing rates remain above the Authority's average long-term borrowing rate of 3.84%. This approach is considered prudent, as long-term rates are forecast to decline further during 2025 and 2026.

findings.headline: Council's own risk assessment: cost pressures persisting through 2024-25 (particularly Social Services and Environment) carry forward risk into 2025-26 without clear mitigation yet in place
findings.detail: Council explicitly flagged that multiple cost pressures persisted through the year or emerged in final quarter and carry forward risk. Requires Budget Holders to develop Action Plans to either mitigate or identify offsetting reductions, but outturn stage suggests these plans are not yet finalised. Pressures identified across Social Services, Environment, and Housing.
findings.matters: Council acknowledging structural pressures flowing into next year without finalised mitigation plans indicates these may not be resolved; suggests forward-year budget risk will require either further reserves or service constraint
findings.figures: Multiple portfolios reporting persistent adverse variances; Council requiring Action Plans to be developed for continuing pressures
findings.quote: While the overall financial position for 2024/2025 is positive, a number of cost pressures have persisted throughout the year or emerged during the final quarter. There is a risk that these pressures will continue into 2025/2026.

findings.headline: Building Cleaning £0.35m adverse variance from back pay following job evaluation and regrading—unusual sign of historical payroll issue settled in-year
findings.detail: Environment portfolio adverse variance of £0.35m attributed to back pay following job evaluation and staff regrading. This is unusual to see in an outturn report and suggests a historical payroll matter was settled or corrected during the year. Portfolio also reports street lighting £0.13m and winter maintenance £0.17m adverse variances.
findings.matters: Back pay and retrospective regrading suggest prior management gaps or historical liabilities; raises questions about other potential undisclosed or unresolved payroll or HR matters
findings.figures: Building Cleaning back pay £0.35m; Street Lighting £0.13m adverse; Winter Maintenance £0.17m adverse
findings.quote: Building Cleaning – An adverse variance of £0.35m due to back pay following job evaluation and staff regrading.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs £0.28m adverse; council identifies affordability and availability pressures in private rental market persisting despite grant mitigation
findings.detail: Housing Services adverse variance £0.28m linked to temporary accommodation. Council attributes this to affordability and availability issues in the Private Rental Sector and No-One Left Out approach. Variance was partially offset by additional Welsh Government grant of £0.617m and use of lower-cost pre-booked rooms, but council explicitly notes demand remains high.
findings.matters: Persistent cost pressure in temporary accommodation despite grant support suggests underlying market shortage; if grant funding reduces or housing shortage worsens, this could become a significant budget pressure
findings.figures: Temporary Accommodation £0.28m adverse variance; Welsh Government grant £0.617m received; demand explicitly noted as remaining high
findings.quote: Housing Services – An adverse variance of £0.28m linked to Temporary Accommodation costs. Contributing factors include affordability and availability issues in the Private Rental Sector and the continuation of the No-One Left Out approach. The variance has reduced due to lower-cost pre-booked rooms and additional Welsh Government grant funding of £0.617m, though demand remains high.

findings.headline: Social Services reporting £1.1m+ in persistent adverse variances driven by placement demand and care complexity, not underfunding
findings.detail: Children's Services £0.3m adverse from increased Special Guardianship Orders and When I'm Ready placements. Community Care £0.5m adverse from increased complexity and domiciliary care packages including double-handed care. Adults learning disabilities £0.1m from agency staffing costs. Other Adult Services £0.2m from employment-related legal fees. These pressures persisted through quarters and into year-end.
findings.matters: Growth in placement demand and care complexity are structural, not cyclical; councils with rising demand patterns face forward budget pressure that cannot be managed through efficiency alone
findings.figures: Children's Services £0.3m adverse; Community Care £0.5m adverse; Adults learning disabilities £0.1m; Other Adult Services £0.2m
findings.quote: Other Children's and Family Services – An adverse variance of £0.3m, primarily due to increased Special Guardianship Orders and When I'm Ready placements. Community Care – An adverse variance of £0.5m, reflecting increased complexity and number of domiciliary care packages, including double-handed care, increased frequency of calls and hospital discharge support.

findings.headline: School sector swung from £1.2m surplus to £1.3m combined deficit, with 10 schools in deficit and council committing £4.89m over 2 years to support recovery
findings.detail: Overall school balances moved from £1.204m surplus in 2023-24 to £1.275m deficit in 2024-25. Secondary (£177k deficit), middle (£1.179m deficit), and special (£448k deficit) sectors all deteriorated. Council will allocate £4.89m phased over 2025-26 and 2026-27 to support schools developing Deficit Recovery Plans. Schools must balance 2025-26 budgets while managing this recovery.
findings.matters: A major service moving to deficit signals structural financial distress in education; the scale of intervention required and ongoing recovery plans indicate future budget pressure and potential constraints on service delivery
findings.figures: £1.275m net school deficit as at 31 March 2025; 10 schools in deficit; combined school deficits £2.516m; £4.890m additional funding commitment phased 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2025, the overall level of school balances has decreased by £2.479m, resulting in a net deficit position across all schools of £1.275m. A total of ten schools were in deficit at year-end, with combined deficits amounting to £2.516m.

news_drafts.headline: Blaenau Gwent capital programme delivers at 86% as council draws on reserves to cover overspend
news_drafts.lead: Blaenau Gwent council spent £41.1m of its £47.7m capital budget in the year to March, a delivery rate of 86.2 per cent, with £6.5m of schemes carried forward into next year. The council reported a net favourable variance of £82,861 on capital spending after accounting for slippage and overspends in four schemes totalling £80,368. External grant funding increased the capital programme by £10.2m since the third quarter, with £9.8m from Welsh Government and Shared Prosperity Fund approvals for four regeneration projects. On the revenue side, the council faced an overall adverse variance and drew £1.4m from its Financial Planning and Resilience reserves to balance the position. The net decrease across all specific reserves was £1.964m, with school balances reduced by £2.051m. The council also set aside £342k for future interest rate hedging.

news_drafts.headline: Blaenau Gwent draws on reserves to cover budget shortfall as capital programme completes early
news_drafts.lead: Blaenau Gwent Council used £1.4 million from its financial reserves to cover an overspend in day-to-day running costs in the year to March 2026, the Corporate Governance and Resources Scrutiny Committee heard on 24 September. The council's specific reserves fell by a net £1.964 million overall, and school balances were drawn down by £2.051 million to help fund the council position. On capital spending, the council spent £41.1 million of its £47.7 million budget, delivering 86.2 per cent of planned projects, with £6.5 million of work carried forward to the next year. Four capital schemes overspent by a combined £80,368, but these were accommodated within available resources. The capital programme achieved a net favourable variance of £82,861 after accounting for the slippage and overspends. The council also approved £6.3 million in Transforming Towns regeneration funding in the final quarter, bringing four major urban schemes into its capital programme.

news_drafts.headline: Blaenau Gwent draws £1.4m from reserves to cover spending overspend
news_drafts.lead: Blaenau Gwent Council is drawing £1.4m from its reserves, money set aside for unexpected costs, to cover an overspend on day-to-day spending, the council's annual accounts for 2025-26 show. The drawdown forms part of a wider erosion: total reserves fell by £1.9m in the year, reducing the council's financial cushion. School balances dropped by £2.1m, with accumulated school surpluses used to support the council's position. The council also set aside £342k to cover potential future interest rate rises on its borrowing. The capital programme, which covers spending on long-lasting assets, performed better: it spent £41.1m of a £47.7m budget and achieved a favourable variance of £83k, though £6.5m in planned spending was carried into the next financial year.
